items.followUp: Define hydrogen bonding and explain it using water as an example.

rubric.why: Identifies the molecules involved.
rubric.description: States that dipole–dipole interaction occurs between polar molecules with permanent dipoles.
rubric.how: Award for identifying polar molecules or permanent dipoles.

rubric.why: Describes the electrostatic attraction that causes the interaction.
rubric.description: Explains that the positive end of one molecule attracts the negative end of another.
rubric.how: Award for stating the attraction between oppositely charged ends; both ends must be identified.

rubric.why: Provides a relevant example and applies the explanation to it.
rubric.description: Gives HCl as an example and identifies attraction between the H end of one molecule and the Cl end of another.
rubric.how: Award for the HCl example and describing the attraction between neighbouring molecules.

modelAnswer: Dipole–dipole interaction is the electrostatic force of attraction between permanent dipoles of polar molecules.
The positive end of one polar molecule attracts the negative end of a neighbouring molecule.
For example, HCl molecules are polar: the hydrogen end is partially positive and the chlorine end is partially negative.
The H end of one HCl molecule is attracted to the Cl end of a neighbouring HCl molecule.

items.followUp: Explain why sweating cools the human body.

rubric.why: Shows that evaporation is not limited to the boiling point.
rubric.description: States that evaporation can occur continuously at temperatures below the boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for saying it occurs continuously or below the boiling point.

rubric.why: Identifies which liquid molecules escape during evaporation.
rubric.description: Explains that higher-energy molecules at the liquid surface escape into the vapour.
rubric.how: Award for identifying surface molecules or high-energy molecules escaping.

rubric.why: Explains the reduction in temperature of the remaining liquid.
rubric.description: States that the remaining molecules have lower average kinetic energy, so the liquid cools.
rubric.how: Award for linking reduced average kinetic energy to cooling.

rubric.why: Accounts for the energy needed for evaporation and its cooling effect.
rubric.description: States that energy is taken from the liquid or its surroundings to enable evaporation.
rubric.how: Award for stating that evaporation absorbs heat from the liquid or surroundings.

modelAnswer: Evaporation occurs continuously from the surface of a liquid, even below its boiling point.
The higher-energy molecules at the surface escape into the vapour.
The average kinetic energy of the molecules left behind decreases, so the liquid becomes cooler.
The energy needed for evaporation is taken from the liquid and its surroundings; therefore, evaporation is a cooling process.

items.followUp: Calculate the mass of KOH needed to prepare 250 cm³ of a 0.20 M solution.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies and converts the given volume and concentration.
rubric.description: Converts 500 cm³ to 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³ and 0.4 mol dm⁻³ to 400 mol m⁻³.
rubric.how: Award for correct SI conversions of the given quantities.

rubric.why: Uses concentration and volume to determine the amount of NaOH.
rubric.description: Uses n = CV and obtains 0.20 mol of NaOH.
rubric.how: Award for the correct formula and amount in moles.

rubric.why: Uses the correct molar mass of NaOH.
rubric.description: States the molar mass of NaOH as 40 g mol⁻¹.
rubric.how: Award for the correct molar mass.

rubric.why: Gives the required mass with a unit.
rubric.description: Calculates the mass of NaOH as 8 g.
rubric.how: Award for the correct final mass and unit.

modelAnswer: Given: C = 0.4 mol dm⁻³ = 400 mol m⁻³; V = 500 cm³ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³.
Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol⁻¹.
Formula: n = CV.
Formula: m = n × molar mass.
m = 0.20 mol × 40 g mol⁻¹ = 8 g.
Therefore, 8 g of NaOH is required.

items.followUp: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten but not when solid?

rubric.why: Identifies the strong forces holding the ions together.
rubric.description: States that oppositely charged ions are held by strong electrostatic attraction in a lattice.
rubric.how: Award for identifying strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: Connects the strong attractions to the energy required for a change of state.
rubric.description: Explains that considerable energy is needed to overcome these attractions, giving high melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award for linking the strong ionic attractions to high melting or boiling points.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds contain oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction in a lattice.
A considerable amount of energy is needed to overcome these forces, so ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points.

items.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of silicon (atomic number 14) according to shells and subshells.

rubric.why: Checks the shell arrangement of aluminium's 13 electrons.
rubric.description: Gives the shell configuration 2, 8, 3.
rubric.how: Award for the correct shell configuration.

rubric.why: Checks the full subshell configuration of aluminium.
rubric.description: Gives the subshell configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹.
rubric.how: Award for the complete and correct subshell configuration.

modelAnswer: Aluminium has atomic number 13, so it has 13 electrons.
According to shells: 2, 8, 3.
According to subshells: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a shell and a subshell, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of a shell and its example.
rubric.description: Defines a shell as a principal energy level and gives an example such as the M shell or third shell.
rubric.how: Award for the shell definition and a suitable shell example.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of a subshell and its example.
rubric.description: Defines a subshell as a subdivision of a shell and gives an example such as 3s or 3p.
rubric.how: Award for the subshell definition and a suitable subshell example.

modelAnswer: A shell is a principal energy level in an atom, for example, the third shell or M shell.
A subshell is a subdivision of a shell, for example, the 3s or 3p subshell.

items.followUp: Describe how atomic radius changes across a period and down a group.

rubric.why: Checks the trend across a period.
rubric.description: States that electronegativity generally increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award for the correct increasing trend across a period.

rubric.why: Checks the trend down a group.
rubric.description: States that electronegativity generally decreases down a group.
rubric.how: Award for the correct decreasing trend down a group.

modelAnswer: Across a period, electronegativity generally increases from left to right.
Down a group, electronegativity generally decreases from top to bottom.

items.followUp: Write two features of the modern long-form periodic table.

rubric.why: Checks the basis of arrangement in the long-form periodic table.
rubric.description: States that elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
rubric.how: Award for stating the increasing atomic-number arrangement.

rubric.why: Checks a structural feature of the table or a property of groups.
rubric.description: Gives a valid feature, such as seven periods, eighteen groups, or similar valence-electron arrangements and properties within a group.
rubric.how: Award for one correct structural or group feature.

modelAnswer: Elements in the long-form periodic table are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
The table has 7 horizontal periods and 18 vertical groups; elements in the same group have similar valence-electron arrangements and chemical properties.
